sections.title: Playing
sections.info: How the piano answers to how hard you play (velocity). These settings change soft and medium notes, and the hardest notes hardly at all. The on-screen keyboard and the computer keys always play one fairly hard velocity (100), so they show little of it: press the graph instead to play the last key at any velocity, soft at the left and hard at the right, or use a MIDI keyboard. The graph shows that key's loudness (solid) and tone (dashed) across velocity, and a dot for each note struck.

sections.title: Space
sections.info: The room around the piano. The measurements are close-miked, so Reverb 0 is the dry piano. Early reflections come from a model of each space; the tail is a smooth feedback network, so Decay, Size and Damping can be set freely.

sections.title: Key Maps
sections.info: Each key's own departure from the piano: its tuning, how far its strings beat against each other, its hammer, level, sustain, damper and string stiffness, as a worn or unevenly kept piano has. Draw a map, or fill them all with Age Piano. Each map moves its keys away from the global settings (Strings, Tone), so those still work. Saved with the patch.

accordion.title: Partial Arp
accordion.info: Not the arpeggiator below: this one plays inside each note. Each note's partials take their turn, a melody inside the note: by default each turn digs them out (Boost below 0 dB: a moving notch); a positive Boost brings them forward instead. Off leaves the piano as measured.

accordion.title: Touch Point
accordion.info: A finger resting on the strings, as a player reaches into a grand to sound harmonics or mute a note. It takes the partials that move under it and leaves those that have a still point (a node) there: at half the string every second partial rings on, an octave up; at a third, every third, an octave and a fifth up. Press 0 leaves the piano as measured. What the finger takes doesn't come back until the key is struck again.

accordion.title: Listening Point
accordion.info: Where along the string the sound is taken, as a pickup on an electric instrument takes it. Each partial is heard as strongly as the string moves at that point: near the end the low partials are weak and the sound thin and bright; towards the middle it turns hollow, and at half the string every second partial is silent. Nothing is taken from the vibration, so the point can move while notes ring: route an LFO or a Shape to Point and the partials rise and fall one after another. Depth 0 leaves the piano as measured.

accordion.title: Hammer Surface
accordion.info: What the hammer is made of. This piano's hammers are felt, which gives under the string: the upper overtones fall away steeply, and more so the softer the strike. Edge, Weight and Core change that, from a simulated hammer on these strings; Hardness (Tone) still softens or hardens the felt itself. With Morph on, Material sets all three at once, from felt through worn felt, leather on a light hammer and wood to metal, and their own knobs aren't read. Wear packs the felt hard where a piano is played most, and Uneven gives every key a hammer of its own; both work on top of the others, with Morph on or off. Each note takes its hammer as it is struck, so a route from velocity, the key or a random value to Material gives every note its own. Loudness is kept. At the defaults the piano is as measured. The on-screen keys play one velocity: press the velocity graph (Playing) to hear soft and loud strikes.

An arpeggiator and step sequencer that play piano notes from the keys you hold. Arp plays the held keys one after another; Sequencer lets each key sound and adds its own pattern of notes above it. Each note is a full piano strike, ended by its damper (Note Envelope Off, the default) or by the note envelope.

Routes from a source (an LFO, a Shape, velocity, the key, a random value per note, the mod wheel, the beat, the arpeggiator's envelopes…) to the piano's controls. Tone and hammer settings are read as each note is struck, so a route there gives each note its own tone; the strings' Sustain, Unison, Dampers and Overtone Decay and the Partial Arp follow it as notes ring; Space and the phrase envelope follow sources shared by all notes (Global LFOs, Shapes on Bar, Beat or Free, the wheel, the beat). Pitch and Level (vibrato, tremolo) move every note.

paramInfo.play.touch: How hard you have to play to get a loud note. Below 0 (lighter touch): soft and medium playing come out louder and brighter, as if you were playing harder. Above 0 (heavier touch): the same playing comes out quieter and darker, and you have to dig in. Listen on soft and medium notes: the curve in the graph bends up or down. The hardest notes don't change.
paramInfo.play.dynamics: How much quieter soft notes are than hard ones. 100% is the recorded piano's own range. Lower: soft notes come up towards the loud ones, for a more even, compressed level (at 25% a soft note is about 11 dB louder). Higher: soft notes drop further away, for more contrast. Only the level changes, not the tone; the hardest notes stay where they are.
paramInfo.tone.bright: Tilts every note's partials: more or less treble per octave of overtones, like harder or softer hammers.
paramInfo.tone.hammer: The strike at the start of each note: the hammer, key and soundboard's own response, as recorded from A2 up (octave bands of noise below). 0 dB is as measured.
paramInfo.string.unison: How far the two or three strings of each note are out of tune with each other: the slow beating in a sustained note, and in the treble the spread of each partial's cluster. 100% is as measured; 0% is a perfectly tuned unison.
paramInfo.string.stretch: The recorded piano's stretch tuning: low notes flatter and high notes sharper, as a tuner sets a real piano to match its stiff strings. 0% is plain equal temperament.
paramInfo.string.sustain: How long notes ring. 100% is as measured.
paramInfo.string.damper: How long the dampers take to stop a note when you let go of the key. Keys above E6 have no dampers, as on a grand (Top Dampers changes that).
paramInfo.space.width: Stereo width of the two microphones the piano was measured with.
paramInfo.space.room: How much of the space you hear. The measurements are close-miked, so 0 is the dry piano.
paramInfo.tone.attack: How long each note takes to swell in at the strike. 100% is as measured for each key, from the recordings.
paramInfo.tone.body: The soundboard and room ringing on after each strike: the echo-like tail most audible on high notes. 0 dB is as measured. The key's damper stops it when you let go (above E6, where a grand has no dampers, it rings on unless Top Dampers is All keys).
paramInfo.play.tone: How much the tone darkens as you play softer. 100% is as recorded: each loudness has the tone the real piano had at that loudness. Lower: soft notes keep the bright, hard-struck tone while staying quiet (0%: every note has the hardest strike's tone). Higher: soft notes turn darker and rounder still. Only the tone changes, not the level; listen on soft and medium notes.
paramInfo.play.softattack: How much more slowly softer notes swell in. 0%: every note starts as fast as measured. Higher: the softer the note, the more gradually it rises, from a slightly cushioned start (around 100%) to a slow swell with no hammer edge, like a bowed note (600%). Hard notes keep their quick start. Listen on soft notes; up to about 100% the change is small.
paramInfo.play.softpedal: The soft pedal (una corda), also on MIDI controller 67. 0% is pedal up; 100% is fully down. Notes struck with it down are quieter and rounder at the start but ring on as long. Up to half way the hammers meet the strings on softer felt; from there each also misses one string of its three. Notes already ringing keep their tone, as on a piano.
paramInfo.play.velmap: How velocity is spread over the piano's range. Smooth: loudness and tone rise evenly from the softest to the hardest touch. As Recorded: the sample library's own 16 velocity steps, unevenly spaced; soft and medium notes come out a little louder and brighter. The hardest notes are the same in both.
paramInfo.tone.mech: The piano's mechanical sounds: each key's own noise as it comes back up and its damper lands, and the sustain pedal's thump going down and up. Measured from the recordings; 0 dB is the level the sample library mixes them at.
paramInfo.string.resonance: Sympathetic resonance: how loudly the strings you aren't playing ring along. It is heard with the sustain pedal down, when every string is free: play a few short notes with the pedal held and listen to the wash that stays behind them. Higher: a fuller, longer halo (at +24 dB as loud as the notes' own tails). Lower: drier; −40 dB turns it off. Without the pedal only the top strings (above E6, which have no dampers) are free, and the effect is very faint.
paramInfo.string.topdampers: A grand has no dampers above E6: those notes ring on after you let go, fading as they would held. All keys: every key is damped on release, as on many digital pianos.
paramInfo.tone.hardness: The hammer's felt. Softer dulls the partials and the strike and swells in more slowly, down to a felt-piano mute at -100%; harder brightens them and swells in faster. It moves the corner of the hammer's spectrum, measured per key and velocity from the recordings, up to three octaves either way. 0% is the recorded piano.
paramInfo.tone.strikepoint: Where along the string the hammer strikes. 12% is each key as recorded; other settings move every key's hammer in proportion. Nearer the end (lower) is thinner and brighter. Further in is fuller and hollower, and at 50%, the middle of the string, the even overtones drop out. Loudness stays the same.
paramInfo.tone.strikedepth: How far Strike Point goes. At 0% the overtones change as far as the recordings support: the realistic hammer. Turning it up exaggerates the change, up to three times: overtones at the hammer's nodes fall silent and the ones between ring out, towards a different instrument. It does nothing while Strike Point is at 12%.
paramInfo.string.stiffness: How stiff the strings are. A stiff string's overtones are sharper than whole multiples of its pitch, which gives a piano its slightly metallic edge. 100% is the measured piano. Lower: the overtones line up and the tone turns smoother and purer, like a harp or an organ (0%: perfectly harmonic). Higher: they spread apart and the tone turns clangorous, towards bells and gongs (800%). It is plainest in the bass and the top octaves, and from about 300% in the middle. It applies to the notes you strike next.
paramInfo.string.overtonedecay: How long the upper partials ring compared with the measured piano, the fundamental's decay kept. Below 0%, they ring on longer (bright, steely); above, they die sooner (dark, like gut or nylon strings).
paramInfo.parp.pattern: The order the partials take their turn: up the series, down, up and back, or at random (never the same twice running). Off turns the arpeggiator off: the piano as measured.
paramInfo.parp.scale: Which partials take part, by the pitch each harmonic has against the note: Major Pentatonic (harmonics 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 16, 18, 20, 24, 27…), Minor Pentatonic (with the 7th harmonic as the flat seventh), Major Triad, every harmonic, or the odd ones only (hollow, clarinet-like). The piano's stiff strings tune the upper partials a little sharp of these.
paramInfo.parp.low: The lowest partial in the pattern (1 is the fundamental). Partials below it, and above Highest, are left as they are.
paramInfo.parp.high: The highest partial in the pattern. High keys have fewer partials: the pattern uses only those the note has.
paramInfo.parp.rate: Steps per second, when Sync is off. Each note starts its pattern when it's struck.
paramInfo.parp.sync: Lock the step length to the tempo, at Division.
paramInfo.parp.division: The step length when Sync is on.
paramInfo.parp.overlap: How long each partial's swell lasts against the step. 100%: it takes two steps, so one partial rises while the last one falls. 0%: each has its step to itself, a pulse. 200%: three at once, a smear.
paramInfo.parp.boost: How far a featured partial moves at its turn, against its natural level. Negative (the default, -20 dB) digs it out: a moving notch, the more natural sound. Positive brings it forward instead, which stands out more but can sound resonant; try Octaves and some Width with it.
paramInfo.parp.others: Where the pattern's other partials sit while it's not their turn. 0 dB leaves them as measured; lower thins the note to the pattern, with the partials outside it (below Lowest, above Highest) carrying on as usual.
paramInfo.parp.group: Single: each step features one partial (sharp, whistle-like when boosted). Octaves: a step is a pitch of the scale, and every partial of it in range moves together (E: 5, 10 and 20), so the melody comes from across the spectrum rather than one sine.
paramInfo.parp.width: Spreads each featured partial to its neighbours within this many octaves either side, fading with distance: a moving formant rather than a single partial. 0: only the featured partials.
paramInfo.space.type: The space: Room (a small room, 0.6 s), Chamber (1.3 s), Hall (a concert hall, 2.2 s), Cathedral (5 s) or Plate (a bright, dense studio plate, 2.4 s, no reflections). Changing it lets the old space ring out.
paramInfo.space.decay: The tail's length against the space's own (its RT60). 100 % is the space as designed.
paramInfo.space.size: Scales the tail's delays: smaller is denser and more metallic, larger is grainier and more spacious. The decay time stays. Moving it while a tail rings bends its pitch a little, like a tape.
paramInfo.space.predelay: A gap before the reverb starts, on top of the space's own distances: a bigger stage, and a clearer attack.
paramInfo.space.damping: How much faster the treble dies than the rest. 50 % is the space's own; 0 % keeps the treble as long as the body (bright, glassy); 100 % makes it die quickly (warm, dark).
paramInfo.space.early: The early reflections' level against the tail: up for a sense of walls close by, down for a tail that blooms on its own.
paramInfo.space.lowcut: Takes the bass out of the reverb only, so low notes don't turn muddy.
paramInfo.space.highcut: Takes the top out of the reverb only, for a softer, more distant space.
paramInfo.touch.press: How hard the finger rests on the string: how fast it stops the partials moving under it. 0 is no finger. Around 100-300 dB/s the note melts into its harmonic over half a second; 500 and more leaves a short ping and then the harmonic; near the top, with a wide finger, the note is a muted thud. Route a Shape, the mod wheel or aftertouch here to touch a note after it is struck (the Late Touch preset).
paramInfo.touch.point: Where the finger rests, as a share of the string's length from its end. 50% is the middle: the octave harmonic. 33.3% leaves every third partial (an octave and a fifth up), 25% every fourth (two octaves), 20% every fifth (two octaves and a third). With Snap off, nearly everything is stopped between those points. Route Random or Key here and each note gets its own harmonic (the Chance Harmonics preset).
paramInfo.touch.width: How much of the string the finger covers. Narrow (around 1%) is a fingertip: clean harmonics. Wider reaches across the upper partials' still points too, so they all fade: darker harmonics, and at 15-30% a strip of felt or the flat of a hand, a mute (the Felt Mute preset, with Snap off).
paramInfo.touch.snap: On, the finger goes to the nearest point that divides the string into whole parts (1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5...), where harmonics are, so Point steps through the harmonics. Off, it rests exactly where Point says, for mutes and for the dull, bell-like sounds between the harmonics.
paramInfo.touch.dry: How much of the finger's damping reaches the ring the note leaves in the piano's body. At 0% the ring stays, as it would in a real piano (the finger is on the strings, not the soundboard): after a mute a faint wash remains. Turned up, the ring stops with the strings: a dry thud. Listen on the Felt Mute preset; on harmonics it makes little difference.
paramInfo.listen.depth: How much of the sound comes from the listening point. 0% is the piano as measured (the sound the bridge and soundboard give). 100% is the point alone; in between, a blend of the two. The note's loudness is kept.
paramInfo.listen.point: Where the sound is taken, as a share of the string's length from its end. Low (2-6%): close to the end, thin, bright and nasal, the fundamental weak. Around 12-25%: fuller, with single partials missing (every 8th at 12.5%, every 4th at 25%). 50%: the middle, hollow, every second partial silent. A still point is subtle in the middle of the range; the sound is in the movement. Route an LFO (Per Voice) or a Shape here: the Wandering Ear and Opening Ear presets.
paramInfo.listen.width: How much of the string the listening point covers. 0% is a single point: every partial up to the top. Wider averages the string's movement, which quietens the high partials: a darker, rounder sound.
paramInfo.string.restrike: What happens when a key is struck while its strings still ring (under the pedal, in fast repeats, or on the top keys, which have no dampers). At 0% the new strike takes over from the old vibration: every repeat sounds the same. Turned up, the new strike is added to what is already ringing, less what the hammer's felt takes, as on a real string: a soft strike no longer cuts off a loud note ringing under it, fast repeats differ from one another and build, and now and then a strike lands against the string's motion and comes out weaker. Listen with the pedal down: play a note hard, then softly; or try the Struck Again preset, where slow dampers do the pedal's work, pressing the velocity graph at its right and then its left.
paramInfo.hammer.edge: How little the hammer's surface gives. 0% is this piano's felt. Higher brings out the upper overtones and the click of the strike, towards a tack or bare wood at 100%, where a note has the same colour at every velocity, only louder. Heard at every velocity, most on soft strikes and from the bass to the middle.
paramInfo.hammer.weight: The hammer's mass. 100% is as measured. Lighter (lower) gives the low overtones less and leaves the high ones: thinner and brighter, towards an early piano, most with Edge up. Heavier (higher) is fuller and rounder. Loudness is kept, so it changes colour only.
paramInfo.hammer.core: A hard core under thin felt. 0% is felt all the way through. Higher makes the felt thinner: soft strikes stay mellow, and from a certain velocity up the hammer hits through to the core and the note turns bright, as Edge does. At 100% every strike reaches it. Around 30-50% the on-screen keys (velocity 100) are past it and soft strikes on the velocity graph are not.
paramInfo.hammer.morph: On: Material sets Edge, Weight and Core together, and their own knobs aren't read. Off: they are set by hand.
paramInfo.hammer.material: With Morph on: what the hammer is made of. 0% felt (the piano as measured), 25% worn felt (bright only when struck hard), 50% leather on a light hammer (thinner and brighter, an early piano), 75% wood (lighter and harder still), 100% metal (a tack in a full-weight hammer: bright and full). A route from velocity or a random value here gives each note its own hammer.
paramInfo.hammer.wear: Felt packed hard by years of playing. 0% is new felt. Higher makes the hammers harder and brighter, as Edge does, most around the middle of the keyboard, where a piano is played most, and a third as much at its ends. Play a scale from the bass to the top to hear it come and go.
paramInfo.hammer.uneven: Every key its own hammer. 0% is an evenly voiced piano. Higher makes some keys' felt softer and duller, others' harder and brighter, and their hammers a little lighter or heavier: always the same on the same key, unlike a random route, which changes with every strike. Play neighbouring keys one after another to hear it.
paramInfo.keys.depth: How far every key map takes its keys from the global settings: 0 % plays the piano as set, 100 % as drawn, 200 % twice as far. Lower to hear the piano before it aged; modulate it to age and restore it as you play.
